extracted.intended_audience: writers of fiction (novelists), students of literary craft, and critics studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the craft decision between pictorial (scene/setting) presentation and dramatic action in novels — how to prepare scenes, handle time, balance romance and realism, choose voice, and relieve the climax. Uses Balzac, Dickens, Stevenson and examples (Eugénie Grandet, Bleak House) to illustrate principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pictorial impression to support drama
rubrics_metrics.description: “a pictorial impression, wrought to the right pitch, will speed the work of drama—will become an effective agent in the book, instead of remaining the mere decorative introduction that it may seem to be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a vivid, comprehensive scene and world in advance so that when action begins it can move rapidly without losing emphasis; the pictorial groundwork provides a reserve of vigour that helps and authenticates the drama. Example: Balzac’s method of furnishing a scene so the action afterwards requires less exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and compression of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac’s skill in compressing ‘so much experience into two or three hundred pages’ by using pictorial preparation rather than long narrative development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When compressing a long sweep of life into a short book, rely on concentrated, well-chosen pictorial detail and an already-established world to imply breadth of experience rather than expanding the narrative length. Avoid unnecessary interweaving purely to create apparent scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring characters across books should not burden a single story
rubrics_metrics.description: The device of making the hero of one story ‘figure more or less obscurely in a dozen others’ may swell the look of a whole oeuvre but in a single story background characters must ‘shed their irrelevant life.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a recurring minor character brings irrelevant past associations into a given story, those associations will ‘detract from the force’ of the foreground narrative. Use recurring figures only insofar as their past is directly relevant to the present action; otherwise mute or simplify their backstory to preserve unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve unity by suppressing irrelevant background associations
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In any single story, such of these people as appear by the way, incidentally, must for the time being shed their irrelevant life; if they fail to do so, they disturb the unity of the story and confuse its truth.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that incidental characters contribute only what is necessary to the main action; avoid introducing extraneous relations between reader and background figures that distract from the protagonist’s point of view or the story’s truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial setting to tone down excessive drama
rubrics_metrics.description: When ‘the dramatic method is too much for [a story]…it must be restrained, qualified, toned down, in order to make its best effect’ by recourse to pictorial description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If action threatens to seem overcharged, romantic, or incredible, interpose pictorial, documentary, or commonplace detail to make the incident seem more natural and believable. Balzac often used setting to extenuate or confirm an incredible story; Dickens achieves smoother integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance truth and romance for coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac’s ‘passion for truth was often in conflict with his lust for marvels,’ producing an ‘open gap’ between the realistic picture and the romantic/dramatic elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sharp contrasts between hyper-realistic detail and wildly romantic plot elements. Either temper the romance or temper the realism so that the method (picture vs drama) remains consistent; Dickens is cited as a better example of integrating both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce violent or romantic drama gradually through populated scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Stevenson noted Dickens’s method ‘to lead gradually into them, through well-populated scenes of character and humour; so that his world is actual, its air familiar, by the time that his plot begins to thicken.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare readers with a lively, believable background of characters and small incidents before unleashing a violent or romantic climax; the familiarity of the scene vouches for the credibility of extraordinary events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer action and dialogue to broad, generalized description when dramatizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Dickens’s picture is ‘presented in the form of scenic action’ and he is ‘always readier to work in action and dialogue than to describe at large.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the goal is drama, show characters in scenes and conversation rather than delivering panoramic summary. This often requires sharper, more crystallized characterization confined to a few moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallize incidental characters sharply when they function pictorially
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Dickens translates his picture into action, he is ‘forced to crystallize and formulate his characters very sharply,’ often by ‘labelling his people with a trick or a phrase.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character will appear only briefly but must contribute to the scene’s life, give them a distinctive trait, phrase, or role that reliably evokes them each time. This is an exigent but effective method for crowded scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose narrative voice to shape picture vs drama balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Rendering a story in the first person can be ‘the value of working the drama into a picture, of passing it through a man’s thought and catching his reflection of it.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select first- or third-person narration with awareness that voice changes how action is filtered: first person may dramatize a scene through a single consciousness or, alternatively, tone down raw action by turning it into remembered impression (examples: Stevenson’s Esmond vs Master of Ballantrae).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed, inventory-like description as legitimate preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac’s descriptions are ‘as plain and straightforward as an inventory’—‘no attempt is made to insinuate the impression of the place by hints and side-lights.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough, explicit description of setting (down to furniture, vases, kitchenware) can establish a secure, enduring scene that supports the story—provided the author truly possesses the image and avoids mechanical listing. The efficacy depends on the writer’s imaginative mastery of the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to incarnate past and motivate present action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Maison Grandet ‘incarnates all the past of its old owner, and visibly links it to the action when the story opens.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the environment an active presence that embodies characters’ histories and shapes events; a well-drawn house or street can supply moral and social foundation for the narrative without extra exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relieve the climax by preparing elements earlier
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The climax ought to complete… It should be free to do what it must without any unnecessary distraction… He saves his climax…from the burden of deliberate expatiation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deal with distracting background facts, associations and expository needs in preliminary picture-work so the climax need only deliver the decisive touch. Prepare motifs, routines and settings in advance so the finale is not overloaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure a sense of time through preliminary scene, not prolonged interiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac’s preliminary picture ‘included the representation of time, secured the sense of it so thoroughly that there is no necessity for recurring to it again.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story spans long durations, create durable routines, atmosphere and setting detail that imply the slow passage of years; this allows the narrator to summarize long intervals (e.g. ‘Five years went by in this way’) without losing the feeling of duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose external vs internal focus according to subject’s psychological depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Eugénie ‘lacks the poetry, the inner resonance’ needed for close interior treatment, ‘it is much better to look at it from outside… and to note the incidents that befell her.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the protagonist has limited inward complexity, prefer an external, pictorial presentation that makes their life intelligible from surrounding detail; reserve extended interior consciousness for characters with rich inner material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incongruous mixtures of gaudy romance with sober factual presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac’s effort to ‘absorb the extravagant tale into a study of actual life’ sometimes fails when ‘his romance remains staringly false in its contrast with his reality.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either tone down sensational plot elements or integrate them into the established reality via pictorial grounding; otherwise the contrast will create an open gap that undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain a single effect by reiteration when subject demands it
rubrics_metrics.description: For subjects like La Recherche de l’Absolu, the book ‘must remain throughout, reiterating one effect with growing intensity’ because variety of incident is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the theme is a progressive intensification (e.g., obsession, ruin), structure the narrative as repeated episodes that escalate the same central effect rather than forcing artificial incident variety.
